articles.title: This tiny pocket-friendly e-reader is packed with frustration and potential
articles.summary: Xteink’s X4 e-reader is more pocketable than Kindles, Kobos, and E Ink smartphones, but comes with a steep learning curve.
articles.body: I’ve used and reviewed dozens of e-readers over the years, but the 5-inch Kobo Mini remains my favorite for one simple reason: It was small. While it lacked useful features like screen lighting and page turn buttons, its size made it an e-reader I actually wanted to carry every day. The $69 Xteink X4 e-reader is even smaller than the Kobo Mini and E Ink smartphones like Boox Palma. It’s satisfyingly pocketable but also frustratingly unintuitive and functionally limited out of the box. That could be a deal-breaker were it not for a growing community of users working to improve it. Like the Kodak Charmera, I was pleasantly surprised at how small the X4 is in person. Its 4.3-inch E Ink screen is only a bit tinier than the Kobo Mini’s 5-inch panel, but the X4’s bezels are much slimmer, making the e-reader feel significantly smaller. The joy of nerding out over the X4’s size was quickly cut short when I tested one of its most compelling features. [Image: The X4 is about half the size of the Kobo Libra 2 (bottom) and much smaller than the discontinued Kobo Mini (middle). When the X4 was announced last December, Xteink shared photos of the e-reader stuck to the back of an iPhone using its MagSafe feature. It made the X4 seem like a better alternative to e-reader cases for those wanting a second screen on their phones, but the odd position of its magnets makes it impossible to stick the e-reader to the back of my iPhone 16 Pro in any usable way. [Image: [Image: It’s an issue that many X4 users have complained about, and in a statement emailed to The Verge, the company explains that “during our early development and testing phase, we worked with a limited range of iPhone models. As a result, on some newer models, the magnetic alignment may not appear perfectly centered.” As a work-around, Xteink includes a pair of magnetic adhesive rings that can be stuck to devices to allow for proper alignment. However, the X4 also extends past the bottom of my iPhone, so instead of trying to awkwardly use the two together, I’ve been using it as a standalone ultra-compact e-reader. At less than 6mm thick, the X4 takes up very little room in the sling bag I carry every day and is protected using a basic magnetic folio-style case that’s included. [Product: Xteink X4 e-reader | The Xteink X4 is one of the cheapest e-readers on the market, but that price comes with some challenges and compromises, including a 4.3-inch E Ink screen with a 220ppi resolution. That’s less than the 300ppi e-paper screens on the latest Kindle and Kobo e-readers. You’ll see jagged edges on fine text if you look hard enough, but it’s enough resolution for a pleasant reading experience. There’s also no screen lighting, so if you’re planning to read before bed, you’ll need a lamp or a flashlight. The lack of a touchscreen is more frustrating. The X4 features several buttons on its right edge and below its display. They’re not labeled, and their functionality varies depending on where you are in the UI. [Image: [Image: Further complicating matters, three of the buttons are two-sided and do different things depending on which side you press. It’s frustrating to try and remember which side of which button you need to press to make a selection, jump back to a previous screen, or simply navigate a list of options. And it’s not helped by the X4’s limited and confusing software. While Boox’s smartphone-size E Ink Palma devices run Android and let you do everything from watching videos to playing games, the X4 is solely focused on reading, with support limited to TXT and EPUB files, plus images like JPGs and BMPs, which I had limited success loading. There’s no built-in bookstore so you’ll need to source your own DRM-free EPUB files. That’s a little easier now, thanks to Amazon recently expanding support for EPUBs, but just getting ebooks onto the X4 feels harder than it could be. [Image: [Image: The e-reader doesn’t mount as a storage device when connected to a computer, and while you’re supposed to be able to wirelessly upload files from a browser over Wi-Fi or your phone, I didn’t have much success in getting that to work. The easiest way is to copy files to a memory card using a USB reader, but that is needlessly complicated by the X4’s microSD card slot that makes inserting and ejecting a memory card difficult without long nails or a paper clip. [Image: The X4’s software and UI is basic at best and frustrating at worst. Navigating menus for changing button functions or other settings is confusing, and customizing the layout of the ebook you’re reading is very limited. Reading ebooks is an okay experience, and I’m always a fan of dedicated page turn buttons. But if you’re familiar with a Kobo or Kindle, you’ll find yourself sorely missing options for adjusting text formatting. You only get two font-size choices, three line spacing options, and no way to increase the margins around text. Images and illustrations in ebooks are simply not displayed, most text formatting is ignored, and while you’re supposed to be able to load and use your own font files, it’s another finicky feature I had no success with. You can jump to different chapters, pages, and bookmarks, or turn on features like auto page turns at set intervals, but doing so requires opening and navigating a series of menus using the X4’s buttons. It feels unnecessarily complicated. It’s an experience you’ll eventually get marginally comfortable with, but not one you’ll ever enjoy. [Image: [Image: Xteink has already released several software updates improving the X4’s UI and usability. Progress has been slow, but because the company hasn’t locked down the e-reader, a growing community has taken it upon itself to improve the X4. Installing CrossPoint Reader on the X4, an open-source alternative firmware, was a simple process that immediately solved many of the pain points of Xteink’s software. CrossPoint simplifies the X4’s UI, expands the options for how ebooks look, and adds onscreen labels for what each button does. It’s also easy to uninstall, but I don’t think I’m ever going to. The X4 will never replace the Kobo Libra 2 I use for most of my reading. A touchscreen, lighting, access to a robust ebook store, and a UI that doesn’t have me pulling my hair out are features I can’t do without. But over the past few weeks, I haven’t left the house without the tiny X4. It’s a welcome alternative to my phone (that always seems full of bad news) if I have a few minutes to while away, despite its frustrations. I don’t like recommending devices that require third-party upgrades to be “fixed,” but the work being done by the X4 community makes the e-reader worth considering if pocketability — and a little tinkering — is your priority. Photos by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: Google accelerates Chrome’s release cycle from every four weeks to two
articles.summary: Google will release updated versions of Chrome every two weeks, starting in September.
articles.body: Starting in September, Google is moving its Chrome browser to a two-week release cycle, instead of the current four-week cycle, or the six-week cycle that existed for the decade before that. > The web platform is constantly advancing, and our goal is to ensure developers and users have immediate access to the latest performance improvements, fixes and new capabilities. Building on our history of adapting our release process to match the demands of a modern web, Chrome is moving to a two-week release cycle. While releases will be more frequent, their smaller scope minimizes disruption and simplifies post-release debugging. And thanks to recent process enhancements, we are confident this shift will maintain our high standards for stability. The change applies to desktop, Android, and iOS, and begins with the stable release of Chrome 153 on September 8th. Beta releases will also move up to a two-week cycle. There are no changes to the Dev and Canary channels, and Extended Stable for enterprise admins and Chromium embedders will continue to adhere to an eight-week cycle.

articles.title: This even smaller credit card-sized e-reader has one tragic flaw
articles.summary: The Xteink X3 is the smallest e-reader you can buy, but you may not want to because of one big compromise.
articles.body: There’s a new smallest e-reader in my life. The Xteink X3 is even smaller and thinner than Xteink’s X4 while also improving on the X4 with refined (but still far from great) software, simplified buttons, and an improved magnetic mount on the back. It’s a better compact e-reader than the X4 if extreme portability is your priority, but its slimmer design comes at a terrible price that’s a potential deal-breaker. Instead of a USB-C port, the X3 charges through an uncommon magnetic pogo-pin connection. That was a heartbreaking discovery while unboxing the new X3 because it actually comes with a handful of improvements that make it a solid upgrade. The X3 is a millimeter thinner, a few millimeters narrower, and over half an inch shorter than the X4. It’s much closer in size to a credit card, but while the X3 is just a bit too big to squeeze inside my slim wallet, I can slip the two into my pocket without noticing any added bulk. [Image: When the X4 first popped up last December, it wasn’t just its size that caught our attention. Xteink promoted the X4 with images of it stuck to the back of a smartphone like a MagSafe battery, seemingly promising an e-reader that went everywhere your phone did and a more versatile alternative to e-reader cases. But the odd positioning of the magnets on the back of the X4 and its size prevented it from properly piggybacking on my iPhone 16 Pro without resorting to applying adhesive metal rings and having it awkwardly hang off the bottom. [Image: The position of the magnets on the back of the X3 allow it to mount perfectly to the back of an iPhone 16 Pro, but they’re not strong enough to maintain a secure connection. I was thrilled to find the X3 fits perfectly on the back of my iPhone 16 Pro, and then once again disappointed to discover its magnets aren’t strong enough to keep it securely in place. Magnetic accessories like PopSockets or the OhSnap Snap Grip have a satisfying “thunk” when attaching them to your phone. Attaching the X3 to my 16 Pro feels more like the devices are exchanging a weak hug. They don’t remain aligned when holding the two together, and on several occasions the X3 fell off my phone while being inserted or removed from a pocket. [Product: Xteink X3 e-reader | The X3 has a smaller 3.7-inch E Ink display than the 4.7-inch panel in the X4, resulting in a slightly higher 250ppi, but the reading experience remains the same and depends on your comfort in focusing on a screen this small. I like sticking to a small font, which demands my reading glasses at all times, but if your eyes prefer a larger font you’ll be frequently turning the page because the X3 can squeeze fewer words on screen. In that case, you’ll be better off with a larger Kindle or Kobo. There’s still no screen lighting or touchscreen functionality, but the X3’s button layout has been improved. There’s now just a single button on either side of the e-reader used for scrolling menus and turning to the next or previous page when reading, plus a pair of two-sided buttons below the X3’s screen for navigating menus and its OS. [Image: Xteink updated the X3’s OS to include contextual onscreen labels above its front buttons, but they only appear on the homescreen. Having to remember which of the two-sided buttons I needed to press to make a selection or jump back to a previous screen was one of my biggest frustrations with the X4. Xteink has improved the software on the X3 and added contextual onscreen labels above those buttons… but only on the homescreen, which feels like a tease. As you navigate other areas of the OS, those labels disappear. The UI is still frequently frustrating and makes it feel like Xteink wants you to earn the right to use an e-reader this small. [Image: [Image: There are a few other software improvements. There are more options for adjusting line spacing that can help squeeze more text on screen and a new function where you can shake the X3 to turn the page. It worked, but felt like an odd alternative to the buttons. Wirelessly transferring books to the X3 from your smartphone using a mobile app also worked now, but it was a convoluted and clunky process and it’s still much easier to just pop out the e-reader’s microSD card and copy ebook files directly to it using a card reader. [Image: The included font choices are limited and don’t look especially great on the X3’s screen. Most of the limitations with the X4’s software, including just two font size choices, persist with the X3. It gives the e-reader a steep learning curve, and it’s absolutely not a device I’d recommend to anyone looking for the polished UI experience of a Kindle. The excellent CrossPoint Reader alternative firmware was the X4’s saving grace, but it doesn’t support the X3 yet. Dave Allie, who spearheaded the original development of CrossPoint Reader, says X3 support is “basically complete,” but its release is still in limbo. (The CrossPoint Reader firmware now officially supports the Xteink X3 and can be installed using this website while the e-reader is connected to your computer.) Despite software and hardware upgrades that feel lacking, I’d still be tempted to recommend the X3 because I simply adore how small it is. It disappears into any pocket I slip it into while still being comfortable to hold and actually read with. It may seem gimmicky, but over the past week alone I’ve finished half a novel while reading in line at checkout, going through a car wash, and waiting at school pickup. I don’t like reading on my phone, and I find the X3 to be a great alternative to dragging my Kobo around. But the lack of a USB-C port is a real pain point. [Image: The X3 sacrificed a USB-C port to slim down, and instead requires a proprietary pogo-pin cable to charge. It does function as a USB port, however, facilitating alternate firmware down the line. During my testing of the X3, I managed to misplace its magnetic charging cable for three days before remembering where I had moved it. With the e-reader’s battery life rated at around two weeks it wasn’t a big issue to misplace the cable for three days, but it could have easily gone missing for a lot longer than that. The company doesn’t recommend using third-party alternatives found on Amazon and only plans to start selling replacement cables later this month. [Image: The X3 (top) isn’t quite small enough to squeeze into a credit card slot in your wallet, but it’s much smaller than a Kobo Libra 2 (bottom) and X4 (middle). In a world where USB-C is now nearly standardized across all devices, having to keep tabs on a proprietary cable feels like too much of an inconvenience. Making the X3 a bit thicker to accommodate a USB-C port or even a wireless charging coil would not have diminished its pocketability or portability in any meaningful way. As much as I want to take the X3 with me everywhere I go, I don’t think I have any room in my heart for a gadget not on the USB-C bandwagon. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge Update, April 27th: Added a link to the CrossPoint Reader website where the alternate firmware can be installed.

articles.title: A touchscreen and light make the new X4 Pro the best version of Xteink’s tiny e-readers
articles.summary: Xteink’s latest pocket-friendly e-reader is its most expensive yet, but the $99 X4 Pro comes with a touchscreen and lighting, so it’s easier to use anywhere.
articles.body: The familiar story with Xteink’s tiny e-readers plays out once again with its new X4 Pro: upgraded hardware held back by frustrating software. The company’s latest tiny e-reader adds a touchscreen and lighting, so choosing it over a Kindle or a Kobo feels like less of a compromise — until you use it. The new touch controls and some welcome software updates do manage to make the X4 Pro easier to use, but frustrations still abound. There’s a happier ending to the story this time, however, as the team behind the excellent CrossPoint Reader software plan to have their alternative firmware ready for the new device at its launch. If you’ve been considering one of Xteink’s e-readers, the X4 Pro is the one to get, even if it’s the most expensive yet. [Image: [Image: The X4 Pro is available for purchase today through Xteink’s online store for $99, making it slightly more expensive than the company’s $79 X3 and $69 X4 models. That also brings the X4 Pro closer in price to the $110 entry-level Kindle featuring Amazon’s polished e-reader experience and on-device access to a well-stocked digital bookstore. The X4 Pro lacks both of those things, but with a 4.26-inch, 800 x 480 E Ink screen, it’s another extremely pocketable device from Xteink that’s slightly smaller and thinner than the company’s first e-reader, and considerably smaller than Amazon’s 6-inch Kindle. [Image: Instead of a USB-C port, the X4 Pro features a magnetic pogo-pin connector on the back. It functions like a standard USB-C port, however, and an adapter (you won’t want to lose) is included. That thin profile means you’ll need to be prepared for a big compromise: There’s no longer an actual USB-C port. You can still benefit from USB-C functionality but will need an adapter to deal with an uncommon magnetic pogo-pin connection. The adapter is included, but I’d still opt for a slightly thicker device with an actual USB-C port. [Image: [Image: On the back of the X4 Pro you’ll once again find embedded magnets so you can attach it to compatible smartphones like a wireless battery. The magnets feel stronger, but still not strong enough to make me confident the e-reader is going to remain stuck to my phone while jostling around in my pocket. The X4 Pro’s size also makes the tiny e-reader awkwardly extend past the bottom of my iPhone 16 Pro when attached, and at this point I think Xteink should just abandon promoting this functionality. Its e-readers are better as standalone devices. [Image: [Image: The added touchscreen allows for a much simpler button layout on the X4 Pro, and I’m glad the company still includes dedicated page turn buttons on each side in addition to being able to tap the edges of the screen. There’s also a power/wake button and, for the first time, a touch button on the front of the e-reader below its screen for jumping back to the e-reader’s homescreen. [Image: The X4 Pro has a touch-sensitive button located beneath its screen, making it very easy to jump back to the device’s homescreen. There’s been some debate about whether or not these tiny e-readers actually need a touchscreen, but after testing the X4 Pro for over a week I think it’s a welcome upgrade for these devices. Even after months of use, navigating the company’s other e-readers using just buttons has never felt intuitive or easy, and it’s held me back from wanting to carry them everywhere I go. Navigating the X4 Pro using screen taps (like we do with the rest of our mobile devices) finally makes it feel like I’m not fighting the e-reader to make it do what I want. But the X4 Pro’s touchscreen doesn’t feel as sensitive or responsive as a Kindle or Kobo when tapping on the screen, and half the time it feels like I have to repeat a tap with a little more pressure for my finger to be detected. I’m hoping that’s something that can be improved through future software updates. [Image: [Image: The added screen light is an excellent upgrade, and even though it’s a bit uneven and definitely a little brighter at the top of the display, you can adjust its intensity and color temperature using sliders that appear when you swipe down from the top of the screen. There are no automatic adjustments or scheduling available yet, but being able to finally use this e-reader in bed without having a lamp on is a game changer, and I can’t see myself going back to Xteink’s older devices that lack lighting. [Image: Xteink has improved and streamlined the X4 Pro’s software to take advantage of the device’s touchscreen, but it can still be frustrating, and it’s completely worth installing the alternative (and free) CrossPoint Reader firmware. Xteink has made a lot of improvements to its bundled software and UI to accommodate the X4 Pro’s touchscreen. The menus have been streamlined and are easier to navigate with touch, and accessing reading settings by tapping anywhere on the page now feels more intuitive. There’s also more flexibility with adjusting text spacing and layout, but out of the box you’re once again limited to just a single font in two different sizes unless you want to jump through hoops to install your own. But you don’t have to suffer with Xteink’s unpolished software. [Product: Xteink X4 Pro e-reader | Of all the X4 Pro’s improvements, the most compelling reason to get Xteink’s latest e-reader is that the easy-to-install CrossPoint Reader software will be available at launch. It’s a free firmware alternative that vastly improves the UI and reading experience of Xteink’s devices. When I tested Xteink’s last e-reader the team behind CrossPoint Reader wasn’t sure when support for the X3 would be released, but Justin Mitchell has since taken over as the core maintainer of the software and told The Verge that X4 Pro support will be available “before any customers are able to order and receive theirs in the states.” CrossPoint Reader is also now a part of Mitchell’s new Free Ink project that counts Xteink as one of its hardware partners, so the firmware should be compatible with all of the company’s future devices at launch. [Image: The X4 Pro is compatible with Bluetooth accessories including Boox’s wireless Tappy remote. If you’ve been on the fence about grabbing one of Xteink’s e-readers, even with a proprietary USB-C connector and a $99 price tag the X4 Pro is the one to get if you prioritize portability. It won’t match the Kindle or Kobo experience even after installing CrossPoint Reader, but even with its limitations it’s still the best tiny e-reader you can buy and a device I already won’t leave the house without. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: Apple says ‘Fold’ and competitors ask ‘how wide?’
articles.summary: With the first foldable iPhone about to arrive, Apple has already proved it has the influence to change the product lines of Samsung, Huawei, and Xiaomi.
articles.body: Apple is almost certain to launch its first foldable iPhone tomorrow, seven years after Samsung’s Galaxy Fold initially went on sale. And while Apple might be a few years late to the party, the run-up to this launch proves that new CEO John Ternus has inherited a company that’s as influential as it’s ever been. Tomorrow’s iPhone event is likely to be a little different than what we’re used to. For one, the arrival of some iPhone 18 models will likely be delayed — the Pros will be available first, but the regular 18 is supposedly set to launch early next year instead. But leaks and rumors have consistently suggested that Apple will instead pair the release of its Pros with the first foldable iPhone, which is likely to be short, squat, and wide, about the size and shape of a passport. If you’ve been following the phone industry this year, that should sound a little familiar. Samsung, Huawei, and most recently Xiaomi have all released passport-shaped foldables over the last few months, creating an emerging form factor that looks likely to stick around, with Oppo and Honor also tipped to have similar products in the works. You might — not unreasonably — ask what Apple’s got to do with this. After all, Huawei’s Pura X Max launched back in April, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 in July, and Xiaomi’s 18 Fold yesterday. The foldable iPhone hasn’t even been officially teased yet, let alone announced, so how could these Android OEMs possibly have copied it? [Image: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 helped define the passport-sized foldable category in the popular consciousness. We’ll never know for certain which manufacturer landed on the idea of a wide foldable first, but there is good reason to think it was Apple. The company has reportedly been working on a foldable iPhone since at least 2017, with leakers tipping the smaller, wider form factor as early as February 2025. Apple’s formidable supply chain — perfected by former CEO Tim Cook — is slow-moving at the best of times, and by the time leakers knew what was coming, it’s likely industry rivals did too. Samsung in particular has probably known of Apple’s plans for some time, since it’s reportedly the manufacturer of the foldable display panel inside the new iPhone. Besides, this is hardly the first time Apple has had this sort of influence. Last year, the iPhone Air triggered a similar early imitation in Samsung’s Galaxy S25 Edge, not to mention other thin and light phones from the likes of Honor, Huawei, and Tecno. Or how about laptops, where March’s MacBook Neo just prompted a string of cheap and often colorful alternatives from the likes of Lenovo, Dell, and Acer. I’m not suggesting that other manufacturers are entirely unoriginal, but they know that when Apple creates a new market, you don’t want to miss out (with rare exceptions — the lack of imitators suggests that just about everyone could tell the Vision Pro wasn’t likely to be a winner). And there’s little reason to think the major Android players were about to force a change themselves. After seven years of Android foldables, the market has been fairly predictable, outside of the slow arrival of trifold models. Most manufacturers settled into producing phones in the same Flip and Fold form factors that Samsung established, and until Apple’s arrival, there had been little sign of change. If anything, Android manufacturers had been moving away from this direction — early foldables from Oppo and Google were closer in shape to the new wide folds, though a little less extreme, but both manufacturers left those designs behind in order to conform to the norms established by Samsung. The main thing that’s changed since then is Apple’s imminent arrival. [Image: The Xiaomi 18 Fold is so far only out in China, but is the best-specced wide fold yet. And Apple entering the foldable market is important. Despite years’ worth of products, Counterpoint estimated that in 2025 foldables made up just 1.6 percent of all smartphone sales. These are niche by any measure. But the same report estimates that shipments will grow by 20 percent this year, with Apple claiming a 28 percent share after just a few months on the market. Apple’s arrival could push the category closer to the mainstream, as it did with others in the past, and Android OEMs are attempting to align themselves to take advantage. From Apple’s perspective, this launch matters for another reason: It’s John Ternus’ first hardware release as CEO. Ternus is a hardware guy, and as the company’s former head of hardware engineering, he can take some responsibility for Apple’s products holding the influence that they do. The test for Ternus will be to maintain that influence, to combine his hardware expertise with the marketing, supply chain, and services sides of Apple to ensure that five, ten years down the line, Apple still has the influence to reshape whole markets simply by entering them.

articles.title: Intel CPUs are reportedly getting a 10 percent price hike in October
articles.summary: Intel is reportedly planning to increase prices for its PC CPUs by 10 percent in October, as component shortages continue to drive up prices.
articles.body: Intel’s PC CPUs may get more expensive in a few weeks, with Digitimes reporting that Intel has a 10 percent price hike planned, following similar increases earlier this year. According to Digitimes, the price hike is part of a shift for Intel toward increasing profitability for its PC CPU business, rather than keeping prices low to try to expand its market share. Digitimes also says Intel may be planning to cut another 5 to 10 percent of its staff, although it may also bring in new hires at the same time. Additionally, the report claims Intel could soon put its Small Core line in end-of-life, but this would mainly impact industrial PCs and IoT tech, not consumer PCs. Intel’s price hike would come just a month after Qualcomm raised its chip prices on September 1st. In July, Intel reported its “strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years,” largely driven by its data center and AI business. Meanwhile, ongoing component shortages have been driving up prices on everything from RAM to laptops and phones, and the higher prices could last for years.

articles.title: A word with a woman who’s trying to pull off a crossbody phone strap
articles.summary: Maybe geriatric millennials just weren’t made for the crossbody lifestyle.
articles.body: Oh, this thing? It’s just a crossbody strap. It’s a fun and youthful way to carry your phone. It’s all the rage with Europeans and young people. I love it, and I definitely don’t feel weird and self-conscious using it. Plus, it’s great to have a $700 investment dangling near your waist while you walk down the street. Kind of a thrill. Stylish? Yeah, I guess it looks pretty cool. Especially when I pair it with an oversized jacket and it kind of bunches the fabric up around my armpit. It’s a pretty seamless addition to my wardrobe since I basically live in Tevas and a pair of athleisure leggings from Target. I am a Target Circle member, in fact. I don’t like to brag about it, but that’s how plugged in I am to the latest fashion trends. Anyway, one of my friends watched me sling the crossbody over my shoulder and said, “I feel like I’m hanging out with Rick Steves.” Convenient? Totally. It’s so easy to grab my phone, wrestle it around so the screen is facing me, and bang out a text without missing a beat. Way easier than just grabbing it out of my jacket pocket. Plus, I always have my phone handy for tap-to-pay. Sometimes I have to lean in and do a mini squat to reach the pay terminal, but that’s a little bonus workout. That’s just the kind of thing you can do when you live a soft pants lifestyle. You know what else? It’s too goddamn dark in bars these days, or they’re making the print smaller on the menus. Maybe both. But that’s not a problem when you have your phone on a crossbody strap. Just hit that flashlight toggle (on purpose, for a change) and you’ve got a handy reading light at your side. Nothing complements the ambiance of a moody cocktail lounge like 50 lumens of bright white LEDs aimed at your receipt while you figure out whether or not a service charge was included. Honestly? It would be useful if the crossbody could hold other stuff, too. Like maybe my keys, some tissues, and a little notebook. Loose change, Carmex, that kind of thing. And maybe I can take my phone out of it when I get home, hang it up on the coat rack, and have it ready to go for my next outing. A crossbody, but a little bigger so it can hold all the stuff you leave the house with. I bet you they sell one at Target.

articles.title: An air traffic control glitch is disrupting flights across the UK.
articles.summary:
Several UK airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted, and others, have grounded departing flights as the National Air Traffic Services (NATS) deals with a “technical issue” affecting its “flight processing system.” NATS adds that its “engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible.”

articles.title: JBL’s soundbar with detachable rear speakers is over $300 off
articles.summary: JBL’s Bar 700 Mark 2 is steeply discounted at Amazon, and includes two rechargeable satellite speakers and a wireless subwoofer.
articles.body: A lot of people are split between getting a nice all-in-one soundbar or spending more for an option that includes rear satellites for immersive surround sound. JBL’s Bar 700 Mark 2 system is one of the most unique options available, shipping with two modular speakers that charge when docked to the soundbar. When detached, the battery-powered (and mountable) speakers can be placed anywhere, lasting for up to ten hours before needing to recharge. If you’re seeking this kind of versatility, you might be pleased to know that the system has been steeply discounted at Amazon, costing $549.99 (originally $899.99). [Product: JBL Bar 700 Mark 2 | The Bar 700 Mark 2 seems impressive on multiple fronts. The main soundbar component offers 7.1 channels, including two tweeters that fire to the side to bounce around audio with Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X content. It offers vastly superior connectivity compared to some similarly-priced options, with HDMI in (with HDR 10 Plus and Dolby Vision passthrough), HDMI out with ARC and eARC support, plus optical audio. The set includes a wireless subwoofer, plus mounts. One of the most appealing use cases for the Bar 700 Mark 2 is bringing one of its satellites with you around your house or apartment so you don’t totally miss out on the action. If the speaker’s battery is running low before you’re ready to return it to the soundbar, you can easily recharge it just by plugging in a USB-C power source. It’s the best kind of sale, one where no offer code is required to save. One of the most interesting products that’s available for less is the SmartCharge Gen 2, a 10,000mAh battery that has two built-in USB-C cables (up to 22.5W charging speed), an Apple Watch-ready wireless charging pad and extra USB ports. Best of all, it has fold-in prongs that let you easily recharge it. * A fantastic deal is happening at Green Man Gaming for those who want to get the trilogy of Final Fantasy VII remakes. It’s offering Steam keys for all three games, including a preorder for Revelations coming April 8th, 2027, for $84.99. I managed to get the price knocked down to $72.24 by entering the code SEP15 at checkout, but results may vary. Either way, it’s a huge savings considering that Revelations alone costs $69.99 to preorder you’ll instantly get access to Intergrade and Rebirth for less than $20. You’ll get instant access to the two titles that are currently available.
